result.summary: The suitors of Helen come to Tyndareus' house from many lands, offering gifts, and Tyndareus binds them all by an oath to defend the winner; Menelaus wins with the greatest gifts. After Hermione's birth, the text turns to Zeus's plan to destroy the race of demi-gods.

scenes.title: The suitors gather for Helen
scenes.summary: Heroes from Phylace, Athens, Crete, Salamis and Euboea send gifts or come themselves to woo Helen at Tyndareus' house.
scenes.stakes: Each suitor risks losing Helen to a rival who offers more.

scenes.title: Tyndareus' oath and Menelaus wins
scenes.summary: Tyndareus takes oaths from all suitors to punish anyone who takes Helen by force. Menelaus prevails by his gifts, while Achilles is still a boy with Chiron.
scenes.stakes: Tyndareus risks violence among the suitors; Achilles' absence decides Helen's fate.

scenes.title: Zeus plans to end the demi-gods
scenes.summary: Helen bears Hermione. Zeus, with the gods divided, plans to destroy the demi-gods and separate gods from men, and a figure carries out his father's counsels.
scenes.stakes: The race of demi-gods and many heroes face destruction in Zeus's plan.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet linking Helen to the Argives, meaning Greeks.

notable_quotes.reason: Tyndareus' oath of the suitors, a key origin of the Trojan War alliance.
Zeus's plan to end the demi-gods and separate gods from men.

analysis.text: The catalogue of suitors sets up the oath that will bind Greek heroes to fight at Troy, linking Helen's marriage to the end of the heroic age.
The wooing by gifts reflects archaic bridal-gift customs, and the list of heroes from many regions shows a pan-Hellenic view of heroic society.

legacy.text: The oath of the suitors became the standard explanation in later Greek literature for why the Greek kings joined the expedition against Troy.

fun_facts.text: The passage survives only in papyrus fragments, hence the gaps (lacunae), including the Berlin Papyrus.

language_notes.text: Bridal-gifts: the suitor's gifts to the bride's father, a Homeric custom (hedna), offered to win a marriage.
The lacuna marks a gap in the damaged papyrus; the text is missing here and the fragments are incomplete.
Tripods: three-legged bronze cauldrons or stands, valued as wealth and given as prizes and gifts.
'Fitting gifts, even wonderful deeds': Aias offers not goods but a promise to drive off cattle and sheep from many places.
Thwarts: the rowers' benches across a ship; 'many thwarts' means a large ship with many oarsmen.
Ogygian sea: an old poetic epithet; Ogygian suggests ancient, primeval. Its exact application here is uncertain.
The translation uses Zeus here, though other lines may use another form; the line says Idomeneus came by divine prompting.
"Unmixed libations" are pure wine poured out to the gods without water, making the oath especially solemn and binding.
"Do aught apart from him" means act independently of the chosen husband in regard to the marriage, that is, interfere with it.
"Neat-ankled" is a fixed descriptive adjective meaning trim or shapely of ankle.
"Mingle storm and tempest" means stirring up war and disaster over the earth to thin out mankind.
The lines are fragmentary; "declaring those things that were, and are, and shall be" describes a figure with prophetic knowledge, likely Apollo-like foresight, but the subject is lost.
The sword sending heroes to Hades alludes to the coming Trojan War, through which Zeus plans to destroy the demi-gods.

context_notes.text: Phylace was a Thessalian town. Protesilaus later was the first Greek killed at Troy, and Podarces took over his command.
Menestheus later led the Athenians at Troy. Peteous was his father.
Aias (Ajax) of Salamis was one of the greatest Greek warriors at Troy, known for his huge shield and long spear.
Idomeneus later led the Cretans at Troy. His grandfather Minos was the legendary king of Crete.
Tyndareus, Helen's mortal father, feared violence among her many suitors, so he bound them all to defend whoever became her husband.
Chiron was the wise centaur who raised heroes, including Achilles, on Mount Pelion.
Achilles, the greatest warrior of the Trojan War, would have outshone every rival had he been old enough to woo Helen.
Demi-gods were the children of gods and mortals; Zeus's plan to remove them is the origin of the Trojan War in this tradition.

literary_notes.text: Menestheus is shown as confident in wealth, trusting gifts over merit; his pride sets up his later failure to win Helen.
The long list of places Aias would plunder shows the scale of his promised gift and typifies Hesiodic catalogue style.
Idomeneus comes in person rather than sending envoys, setting him apart from earlier suitors who only sent gifts.
Zeus's prompting hints that the gathering serves a larger divine plan, ultimately the Trojan War.
Menelaus wins by wealth rather than prowess, subtly presenting him as a rich, practical suitor despite the epithet "warlike."
The mention of Achilles hints at the later war, in which the greatest hero would have been a rival for Helen.
"Toil and sorrow upon sorrow" pictures suffering as burdens heaped up by Zeus on the heroes.
